**7h**

I started the project thinking it would be easy to quickly sketch out what I had in mind: a converter from a 3.5 mm

![1000012847](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/ksX9hopTccFlCIaHXzVm1PZCSGSdh7qw/a80a5f64a72c6995cdc5d49f38318df2933944a13a1f0dcbcc199c1f16f05367.jpg)

jack socket to a USB Type-C one. I searched for a model and tried to make one from scratch. After some searching, I came across a more specific design with a PCM2912A chip. The model was very hard to find. I also created accounts on Component Search Engine and Ultra Library, but it was all in vain. My account on Component Search Engine kept glitching and I couldn't download anything, so I started from zero.

I looked up tutorials on YouTube and got to work. At first I entered the pins manually (see the first image, where everything was chaotic), but then I used a hotkey that let me do everything in table form (see image 2). The result was that everything was lined up one under the other, which wasn't good (see image 3). After inserting all the pins, I used the X and Y coordinates and left/right settings to change the pin positions. Once I did that, I connected everything with a rectangle, then saved my work and went into the Footprint Editor, where I assigned everything the chip needed (see image 4).

After that, I went into the Schematic Editor, imported the file with the chip, and imported the other necessary components from the KiCad library. While adding parts, I also changed component values to avoid the risk of short circuits. I looked at the datasheet, then at YouTube, then back at KiCad. Progress was very slow because it's my first time using KiCad and I have no idea what's going on in there. I made many mistakes, some very basic and silly, but thank goodness for YouTube (see image 5).

I took breaks at 2 PM and 5 PM, planning to continue working from 5 to 7:40 PM. Now it's 8 PM and I'm writing down what I did, with the project sketch almost finished (see image 6).

### 2026-10-11 – I started working on completing my project at around 4 PM European time, thinking that it would be very easy to finish everything I had to do. I started by correcting some minor mistakes, such as conn

**4h**

I started working on completing my project at around 4 PM European time, thinking that it would be very easy to finish everything I had to do. I started by correcting some minor mistakes, such as connecting certain resistors and fixing other issues related to connecting components to pins (see Image 1). After finishing these corrections, I ran the Electrical Rules Checker to see what errors remained (see Image 2). Obviously, I had a few problems related to the GND label, but I managed to fix most of them (see Image 3).

After about another two hours of work, I managed to connect the jack connector to the rest of the circuit, obviously encountering many errors and problems, which I never seem to escape. Eventually, I managed to fix all the issues mainly related to connecting the components to each other.

Now, the only thing left to do is the PCB itself. I need to move from the electrical schematic to the PCB layout (see Image 3).

I worked intensively during these four hours and did not take any breaks because I am dedicated to finishing the project so that I can submit it.

### 2026-10-11 – I started working on the project and realized that I needed a 1 MΩ resistor (R4) between the XTO and XTI pins of the chip. I added it by pressing the A key on the keyboard and then searching for R in

**1h**

I started working on the project and realized that I needed a 1 MΩ resistor (R4) between the XTO and XTI pins of the chip. I added it by pressing the A key on the keyboard and then searching for R in the search bar. After placing the resistor, I ran the Electrical Rules Checker from the Inspect menu, and it reported an error because I had placed it incorrectly, potentially putting all the components on the PCB at risk of being damaged.

I started looking for tutorials on YouTube and asked an older friend how to arrange everything correctly. He showed me what I had done wrong, and the error disappeared.

### 2026-10-11 – During these two hours, I continued running the Electrical Rules Checker. It reported many errors related to pin 24, which is a power pin, pin 2 (VBUS), and pin 4 of J1. I kept getting errors and did

**2h**

During these two hours, I continued running the Electrical Rules Checker. It reported many errors related to pin 24, which is a power pin, pin 2 (VBUS), and pin 4 of J1. I kept getting errors and did not understand why.

I went to YouTube, and after watching two videos, I found the solution: a power flag, more specifically PWR_FLAG. I placed these flags wherever I was getting errors. That is basically what I did during these two hours. The process was complicated and slow because I did not know how to fix the errors.
